==Problem 24==
The digits <math>1</math>, <math>2</math>, <math>3</math>, <math>4</math>, and <math>5</math> are each used once to write a five-digit number <math>PQRST</math>. The three-digit number <math>PQR</math> is divisible by <math>4</math>, the three-digit number <math>QRS</math> is divisible by <math>5</math>, and the three-digit number <math>RST</math> is divisible by <math>3</math>. What is <math>P</math>?

<math>\textbf{(A) }1\qquad\textbf{(B) }2\qquad\textbf{(C) }3\qquad\textbf{(D) }4\qquad \textbf{(E) }5</math>

==Solutions==
===Solution 1 (Modular Arithmetic)===
We see that since <imath>QRS</imath> is divisible by <imath>5</imath>, <imath>S</imath> must equal either <imath>0</imath> or <imath>5</imath>, but it cannot equal <imath>0</imath>, so <imath>S=5</imath>. We notice that since <imath>PQR</imath> must be even, <imath>R</imath> must be either <imath>2</imath> or <imath>4</imath>. However, when <imath>R=2</imath>, we see that <imath>T \equiv 2 \pmod{3}</imath>, which cannot happen because <imath>2</imath> and <imath>5</imath> are already used up; so <imath>R=4</imath>. This gives <imath>T \equiv 3 \pmod{4}</imath>, meaning <imath>T=3</imath>. Now, we see that <imath>Q</imath> could be either <imath>1</imath> or <imath>2</imath>, but <imath>14</imath> is not divisible by <imath>4</imath>, but <imath>24</imath> is. This means that <imath>Q=2</imath> and <imath>P=\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 1}</imath>.

~CHECKMATE2021

Editor's note: If you are in a time constraint and can't get through the whole problem, you can, with this modular arithmetic,  eliminate the ones' you know can't be in the first position.

===Solution 2=== 
We know that out of <imath>PQRST,</imath> <imath>QRS</imath> is divisible by <imath>5</imath>. Therefore <imath>S</imath> is obviously 5 because <imath>QRS</imath> is divisible by 5. So we now have <imath>PQR5T</imath> as our number. Next, let's move on to the second piece of information that was given to us. <imath>RST</imath> is divisible by 3. So, according to the divisibility by 3 rule, the sum of <imath>RST</imath> has to be a multiple of 3. The only 2 big enough are 9 and 12 and since 5 is already given. The possible sums of <imath>RT</imath> are 4 and 7. So, the possible values for <imath>R</imath> are 1,3,4,3 and the possible values of <imath>T</imath> are 3,1,3,4. So, using this we can move on to the fact that <imath>PQR</imath> is divisible by 4. So, using that we know that <imath>R</imath> has to be even so 4 is the only possible value for <imath>R</imath>. Using that we also know that 3 is the only possible value for 3. So, we have <imath>PQRST</imath> = <imath>PQ453</imath> so the possible values are 1 and 2 for <imath>P</imath> and <imath>Q</imath>. Using the divisibility rule of 4 we know that <imath>QR</imath> has to be divisible by 4. So, either 14 or 24 are the possibilities, and 24 is divisible by 4. So the only value left for <imath>P</imath> is 1.  <imath>P=\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 1}</imath>.

~CHECKMATE2021

===Solution 3=== 
We can simply try each of the answer choices, and we will see which one works. Trying <imath>P=\boxed{\textbf{(A) }1}</imath>, if <imath>PQR</imath> is divisible by <imath>4</imath>, <imath>QR</imath> must be divisible by four. Therefore, <imath>QR</imath> can only be <imath>24</imath>, <imath>52</imath>, or <imath>32</imath>. However, since <imath>QRS</imath> is divisible by <imath>5</imath>, <imath>S = 5</imath>, so <imath>QR</imath> cannot be <imath>52</imath>. When <imath>QR = 32</imath>, <imath>R = 2</imath>, the last requirement cannot be satisfied because <imath>R + S + T = 2 + 4 + 5 = 11</imath>, and <imath>11</imath> is not divisible by <imath>3</imath>. However, when <imath>QR = 24</imath>, <imath>R = 4</imath>, the last requirement can be satisfied. Hence, we can see that when <imath>P=\boxed{\textbf{(A) }1}</imath>, there is one way to satisfy all three requirements, leading to a conclusion that <imath>P</imath> is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }1}</imath>.
